```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 3.2, fig.align = "center")
```

`karma2d` implements the two-dimensional Kumaraswamy autoregressive moving
average (2-D KARMA) model for images whose pixels take values in a bounded
interval, such as vegetation indices, reflectances or proportions. Each pixel
follows a Kumaraswamy distribution parametrized by its **median**, and the
median follows a spatial ARMA structure over the pixels above and to the left
of it. This vignette walks through a complete analysis: simulate, fit,
inspect, predict, check residuals and compare model orders.

## Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("VitorBSP/2d_karma_package")
```

```{r library}
library(karma2d)
```

## Simulating an image

We simulate a 30 x 30 image from a KARMA(1, 1) model. An order-`p`
autoregressive part has `(p + 1)^2 - 1` coefficients, so order 1 has three AR
and three MA coefficients. Their lags can be inspected with `karma2d_lags()`;
the first lag is the **row** lag and the second the **column** lag.

```{r lags}
karma2d_lags(1)
```

```{r simulate}
y <- karma2d_simulate(
  nrow = 30, ncol = 30,
  alpha = 0.1,
  ar = c(0.3, 0.2, -0.1),   # phi(0,1), phi(1,0), phi(1,1)
  ma = c(0.2, 0.1, -0.1),   # theta(0,1), theta(1,0), theta(1,1)
  shape = 10,
  seed = 2024
)
range(y)
image(t(y[rev(seq_len(nrow(y))), ]), main = "Simulated KARMA(1, 1) image",
      col = hcl.colors(32, "viridis"), axes = FALSE)
```

## Fitting the model

`karma2d_fit()` maximizes the conditional log-likelihood with BFGS using the
analytic score. The `order` argument is `c(p, q)`.

```{r fit}
fit <- karma2d_fit(y, order = c(1, 1))
fit
```

The `summary()` method adds standard errors based on the conditional Fisher
information, Wald tests, AIC and BIC.

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

Standard S3 accessors are available:

```{r accessors}
round(coef(fit), 3)
logLik(fit)
nobs(fit)
```

Wald confidence intervals come from `confint()` (which uses
`stats::confint.default()` and therefore the normal approximation):

```{r confint}
round(confint(fit, level = 0.95), 3)
```

## Fitted values and prediction

The conditional likelihood does not model the first `w = max(p, q)` rows and
columns, so `fitted()` is `NA` there:

```{r fitted}
sum(is.na(fitted(fit)))
```

`predict()` returns the fitted median for a new (or the same) image. With
`padding = "none"` the border pixels remain `NA`; with
`padding = "duplicate"` the image is padded as described in the article (first
rows and columns copied above and to the left), so that every pixel gets a
prediction.

```{r predict}
pred_none <- predict(fit)
pred_pad  <- predict(fit, padding = "duplicate")
c(NA_none = sum(is.na(pred_none)), NA_padded = sum(is.na(pred_pad)))

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
image(t(y[rev(seq_len(nrow(y))), ]), main = "Observed", axes = FALSE,
      col = hcl.colors(32, "viridis"), zlim = range(y))
image(t(pred_pad[rev(seq_len(nrow(pred_pad))), ]), main = "Predicted median",
      axes = FALSE, col = hcl.colors(32, "viridis"), zlim = range(y))
par(op)
```

Predictions can also be made on the linear-predictor scale with
`type = "link"`, and for other images with `newdata`.

## Residual diagnostics

Quantile residuals are $\Phi^{-1}(F(y \mid \hat\mu, \hat\varphi))$. If the model
is adequate they should be approximately standard normal and spatially
uncorrelated.

```{r residuals}
r <- residuals(fit, type = "quantile")
rr <- r[is.finite(r)]
hist(rr, breaks = 25, freq = FALSE, main = "Quantile residuals",
     xlab = "residual")
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
```

`karma2d_diagnostics()` summarizes the residual moments and the spatial
autocorrelation at the first-order lags:

```{r diagnostics}
karma2d_diagnostics(fit)
```

## Comparing model orders

Because every fit uses the same pixels only when the effective region is the
same, compare orders with the same `w = max(p, q)`. Here KARMA(1, 0) and
KARMA(1, 1) both have `w = 1`, so their likelihoods are computed on the same
841 pixels and AIC is comparable.

```{r aic}
fit10 <- karma2d_fit(y, order = c(1, 0))
data.frame(
  model = c("KARMA(1,0)", "KARMA(1,1)"),
  npar = c(length(coef(fit10)), length(coef(fit))),
  nobs = c(nobs(fit10), nobs(fit)),
  logLik = c(logLik(fit10), logLik(fit)),
  AIC = c(AIC(fit10), AIC(fit)),
  BIC = c(BIC(fit10), BIC(fit))
)
```

Models with a different `w` condition on different borders and are fitted to
different numbers of pixels, so their AIC values should not be compared
directly.

## Other supports and links

Images that are not in $(0, 1)$ are handled with the `lower` and `upper`
arguments (for instance `lower = -1, upper = 1` for NDVI). All pixel values
must lie strictly inside the support. The link function can be `"logit"`
(default), `"probit"`, `"cloglog"` or `"cauchit"`. The Kumaraswamy
distribution in the median parametrization is also available on its own
through `dkuma()`, `pkuma()`, `qkuma()` and `rkuma()`:

```{r kuma}
qkuma(0.5, median = 0.3, shape = 4)   # the median is recovered
```
